newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe platinum mine brings boom times.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe platinum mine brings boom times.

text.p: Two years ago Chegutu was just a sleepy stopover for travellers on the highway from Zimbabwe's capital Harare to the second city of Bulawayo.
Now it is bustling with activity. Builders are busy finishing two new suburbs which have sprouted in the past year and the town centre is doing brisk business.
The source of the town's new life is the giant Hartley Platinum Mine, whose huge construction cranes and buildings dominate the skyline 20 kms (14 miles) to the northeast.

The mine, a joint venture between Australian mining giants Broken Hills Proprietary Limited with 67 percent and Delta Gold NL with 33 percent, is Zimbabwe's single largest investment since the southern African country won independence from Britain in 1980.
NEW INVESTMENT

The mine, developed at an estimated cost of about $280 million, hopes to process 2.16 million tonnes of ore per year to produce 150,000 ounces of platinum, 110,000 ounces of palladium, 11,500 ounces of rhodium and 23,000 ounces of gold as well as some nickel and copper.
The mine will make Zimbabwe a major platinum producer, accounting for 3.5 percent of global output, but still dwarfed by South Africa which produces more than 52 percent.
"We are happy about the Hartley project taking place in Chegutu. It has changed the landscape of our area," said Chegutu rural council chairman Fanuel Majome.
"It has provided employment for many of our youths who couldn't find jobs," Majome said.
NEW JOBS

The mine has so far generated employment for 2,900 people, many of them from the surrounding area. About 2,200 work directly for BHP and the rest for contractors constructing the mine, which should start output next June.

"The mine has made a lot of difference for our town. Look at all those new houses that have been built in the space of a year," said one Chegutu resident pointing at some 75 houses the mine built for some of its managers.
It has also built more than 100 homes for the miners.

Chegutu businesses are not the only ones who have benefited from the mine. Along the Harare-Bulawayo highway, about 10 km before Chegutu, the small two-store town of Selous mirrors the transformation of the landscape surrounding the mine.
Travellers on the highway used to speed past the little shops with their crumbling walls.
Now the business have expanded to include a takeaway and restaurant to tap business from the mine workers.
"The construction of the Hartley Mine has provided a tremendous boost to our business," said Timothy Shoko, owner of Highway Takeaways, one of the little shops.
"Since these people have to come in and out of the mine every day, that means lots of customers for us," he said.
NEW CUSTOMERS

Shoko said he resigned from a well-paying job as deputy general manager of the country's largest cotton firm, the Cotton Company of Zimbabwe, to help his wife Jane, -- who also resigned from a job in Harare -- to run the Selous shop.
"I put in all the terminal benefits I got from the Cotton Company into extending this shop into a restaurant and a conference room to cope with business from the mine," he said.
"It was not a wasted investment," he said proudly as the restaurant filled with a crowd of customers, most of them from Hartley.
Shoko said he planned to add a swimming pool and a large barbecue to "make this the entertainment place for Hartley workers".
"My takings have quadrupled. My wife and I have no regrets at all about resigning our jobs in Harare to come here and expand our shop," Shoko said with a satisfied chuckle.
